newsitem.title: IRAQ: Russian Baghdad diplomat backs Iraq on no-fly zones.
newsitem.headline: Russian Baghdad diplomat backs Iraq on no-fly zones.

text.p: Russia does not recognise U.S. and allied no-fly zones in Iraq's north and south and Baghdad has every right to shoot at warplanes enforcing them, a Russian diplomat in Baghdad said on Sunday.

"We do not recognise either of the no-fly zones, in the north and south...This country has the right to protect itself. When they (Iraqis) have warplanes of another country flying over their airspace they have the right to shoot," Vladimir Titorenko, deputy head of the Russian mission in Baghdad, told Reuters in an interview.
Iraq said on Friday it would halt firing missiles at U.S. and allied warplanes for the time being to defuse the latest military showdown with Washington over the air-exclusion zones.
The United States is continuing with its military buildup in the region, ferrying more troops and assault planes for further possible attacks against Iraq.
Titorenko said Moscow saw the dispatch of more U.S. troops to the region as an attempt by Washington to escalate tension.

"The continuation of bringing troops here and bringing more airplanes is not a good sign of course...There is no reason to continue strengthening the military presence in the Gulf...We are trying at least to calm down both sides," he said.
He said President Bill Clinton was massing troops in the region so he could win a second term as U.S. president in the election in November.

Russia did not believe Iraq constituted a threat to its neighbours anymore following the dismantling of its nuclear, biological and chemical weapons as well as its long-range missiles by the U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM).

Titorenko said Russia and other countries, which he did not name, were "active in pushing Iraq towards the implementation of resolution 687. We have a good chance to get rid of the remnants of the so-called weapons file."
Resolution 687 sets the terms of the 1991 Gulf War ceasefire. It compels Iraq to scrap weapons of mass destruction in return for the lifting of a ban on its vital oil exports.

Moscow was in constant contact with Iraqi leaders. "They listened to our advice and pulled their troops from the north. Then they listened to our advice not to shoot at U.S. warplanes until we manage to settle the whole situation by political means."
He said he believed Iraqi leaders would honour their pledges and were keen to defuse the situation.
The crisis with the United States started after Iraqi troops moved into the country's Kurdish north to help a Kurdish faction oust rivals from the area.
The move prompted Clinton to mount two missiles strikes against targets in southern Iraq, drawing condemnation from Moscow and criticism from many other countries.
"They (Iraqis) are very cooperative with us. But of course we cannot demand concessions from only one side. The United States should also show more restraint in its actions," he said.
Titorenko said his country had "big financial, economic and strategic interests in this region and Iraq is a very important player in the Gulf."
Russia attempts to spare Iraq another U.S. strike were necessitated by Moscow's concerns "for the respect of international legitimacy".
"Iraq has never committed anything this time against international law," he said.
